title: The guest at the hermitage
hookLine: Shakuntala misses a guest at the gate and a curse follows: why Hindu homes treat the guest as God
carry: the guest is treated as god
last: A CHILD IS YOUR OWN SELF, BORN AGAIN.

lines: A WHOLE PLOT TURNS ON A GUEST.
cards: A sage stands at the gate of a forest hermitage and calls out. Inside, a young woman sits lost in thoughts of her husband, and doesn't hear him.

That missed welcome sets off a curse, a lost ring, and a king who forgets his wife. It's Shakuntala again, but not as the Mahabharata tells it. This is the poet Kalidasa's play, and its whole plot turns on a guest.

teach.h: IN THE EPIC, THE KING CHOOSES TO FORGET
teach.b: In the epic, Shakuntala tells the king the truth, a voice from the sky backs her, and the king says, in paraphrase, that he knew her all along, but wanted his people to hear it from heaven so no one would doubt the child.
There, the forgetting is a choice.

teach.h: IN THE PLAY, A GUEST NO ONE GREETED
teach.b: In Kalidasa's play, the sage Durvasa, well-known for his temper, arrives at the hermitage. Shakuntala, dreaming of the king, doesn't greet him. So he curses her: the one you're thinking of will forget you.
A friend begs for mercy, and the curse is softened: a token will bring the memory back. The token is the ring, and the ring slips into a sacred pool. Why would a missed greeting matter so much?

Kalidasa's audience would have known why. An old Upanishad, the Taittiriya, gives a student a parting list: treat your mother as a god, your father as a god, your teacher as a god, and the guest as a god.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS GOD
teach.b: Atithi devo bhava. A guest at the door is met with water, a seat and food. Shakuntala's fault isn't cruelty.
It's love so wrapped up in itself that it misses the person standing at the gate, and many readers take that as the play's quiet lesson.

teach.h: THE RING, THE FISH, THE BOY BHARATA
teach.b: In the end, a fisherman finds the ring inside a fish, the king remembers, and at last he finds their son prying open a lion cub's mouth to count its teeth.

In the epic the boy is named Bharata, and the royal line takes its name from him. Tradition hears his name in Bharat, one of India's own names for itself, though other stories lay claim to that name too.

how: Many Hindu families still greet a guest with water, a seat and food before anything else; Kalidasa's play about Shakuntala is still read, staged and danced in India and beyond.

o: a wife who threw her ring in a river to forget a king
a wife cursed because she didn't greet a guest at the gate
a queen who turned a sage away from the palace door

games.q: the guest at the gate — tap the pairs.
p: the guest she failed to greet
treat the guest as a god
the token that brings memory back
the boy who gives the royal line its name

s: the ring and the fish are in the Mahabharata's telling
they come from Kalidasa's play. in the epic, there's no ring and no curse.
Durvasa curses Shakuntala because she insults him on purpose
she doesn't notice him at all. her mind is on the king, and a guest goes unwelcomed.
'treat the guest as a god' comes from an Upanishad
the Taittiriya Upanishad's parting advice to a student: atithi devo bhava.

games.q: you're Shakuntala in Kalidasa's play. a sage arrives at the hermitage, but your mind is far away with your husband. what happens?
o: you greet him, and all is well.
you don't notice him, and he curses you.
games.why: she doesn't greet him, and Durvasa curses her: the one she's thinking of will forget her. where the guest is treated as a god, a missed welcome is serious. a friend's plea softens the curse so a token can break it.

practice: Think of the next person likely to come to your door. In many Hindu homes a guest is offered water before anything else is said. Picture yourself looking up and handing them that glass, as if God were at the door.
If you pray, ask to see God in whoever comes today. If you don't, simply hold the wish to really see them.

wordCard.voice: Shakuntala. In Kalidasa's play she misses a guest at the gate, and Durvasa's curse makes the king forget her until a ring comes back in a fish.

orig.note: Sanskrit. the Mahabharata explains her name itself: as a baby in the forest, she was guarded by shakunta birds.

carryVoice: Your line: the guest is treated as god. Shakuntala missed one, and the whole story turned. See you tomorrow.
